The first batch of CrCoNi alloy samples was printed by a customized LPBF machine equipped with a 200 W SPI fiber laser source, as schematically shown in Fig. 1a. In contrast with the continuous-wave lasers used in typical LPBF processes, the laser in this work was emitted in repeated pulses at a frequency of 1000 kHz (Fig. 1b). The working duration of each pulse was ∼250 ns. The wavelength and the spot size of the laser were 1060 nm and 100 lm respectively.

To compare the effect of continuous-wave and pulsed-wave lasers on microstructure and mechanical properties, a second batch of CrCoNi samples was printed with the same geometric size using a commercial LPBF machine (EOS M290). The continuous-wave laser used in this batch had the same wavelength (1060 nm) and spot size (100 lm) as the pulsed-wave laser used in the first batch. To decouple the influence of other factors, the print parameters were selected from the process window optimized in the first batch print: a laser power of 200 W, a scanning speed of 500 mm/s, a hatch spacing of 80 lm, a layer thickness of 40 lm, and a scan rotation of 90°.

To validate the effectiveness of the pulsed-wave laser for alloying refractory elements, a third print batch was performed by blending pure CrCoNi powder with different amounts of pure W powder (3 wt% and 10 wt%) with similar particle sizes of 20–45 lm. The maximum amount of blended W powder was set as 10 wt% to avoid the formation of a detrimental secondary phase [19]. The in-situ alloyed (CrCoNi)100-xWx alloy samples were printed using parameters selected from the optimized process window for printing pure CrCoNi alloy.
